s: An iron house shipped whole from Belgium, unlived-in
w: Cast and shipped from Belgium, this iron house was bolted together in 1892 to serve as the governor's residence in what was then Lourenço Marques. No governor ever moved in; the building passed between institutions instead, and today stands open as a rare example of experimental colonial ironwork architecture.

s: A colonial finance office, refilled with books
w: Designed in 1904 by architect Mário Veiga as the colony's Finance Office, this Baixa landmark on Avenida 25 de Setembro now holds Mozambique's national library. The bureaucratic shell of Portuguese Lourenço Marques survived intact through independence, simply refilled with the country's books instead of its ledgers.

s: A cultural house founded by Mozambique's top novelist
w: Named for their father and founded in 2015 by Mia Couto, Mozambique's best-known novelist, with his brothers Fernando Amado and Armando Jorge, this centre occupies a building by architect Pancho Guedes in Sommerschield - a small library, a cafe and a stage where the country's writers and musicians still show new work.

s: One of the world's most beautiful railway stations
w: Built between 1908 and 1916 in full Beaux-Arts style, Maputo's Central Railway Station is regularly ranked among the world's most beautiful. It anchored the CFM Sul line to South Africa, Eswatini and Zimbabwe - a closed line now, but the terminal still commands the square.

s: A 1934 villa that housed the colonial secret police
w: Built in 1934 as an ordinary residence, Vila Algarve spent its final years under Portuguese rule as headquarters of the secret police, PIDE/DGS, until independence closed that chapter. The house survives, listed and quiet, at Avenida Mártires da Machava and Avenida Ahmed Sekou Touré - its past still attached.

s: A colonial fort now holding a king's remains
w: Built from reddish stone at Praça 25 de Junho, this fort centres on a single courtyard reached through one gate. An equestrian statue of Mouzinho de Albuquerque, moved here from outside the old Lourenço Marques municipality, now shares the courtyard with the remains of Gungunhana, brought back from the Azores in 1985.
